title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
Hardware compute roughly doubles based on the Moore’s Law. Deep learning’s appetite has been growing several times faster. That gap is the entire reason this field exists, and everything below is a consequence of it.
The target hardware in this course is the edge: Nvidia Jetson AGX at the top end, microcontrollers at the bottom.

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
Vocabulary used throughout

weights = parameters
neurons = features = activations

Trade-offs in Neural Network design:



Wide and shallow
Narrow and deep




Fewer kernel launches
Better accuracy

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
Basic building blocks of CNNs

The four layer shapes









Layer
Input
Weight
Output




Linear
(n, C_i)
(C_o, C_i), bias (C_o)
(n, C_o)


Conv
[B, C_i, H, W]
[C_o, C_i, k_h, k_w]
[B, C_o, H_o, W_o]


Grouped conv
[B, C_i, H, W]
[C_o, C_i/g, k_h, k_w]
[B, C_o, H_o, W_o]


Depthwise conv
[B, C_i, H, W]
[C_o, 1, k_h, k_w]
[B, C_o, H_o, W_o]



Depthwise is just grouped conv taken to its limit: g = C_i = C_o, so each kernel sees exactly one input channel.
Padding mostly used: zero, reflection (like mirror), and replication (replicate the last digit).

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
Receptive field
Stack L layers of K \times K convolution at stride 1 and the receptive field is
R_L = L \cdot (K - 1) + 1






Growing the receptive field on a budget



Notice that stacking layers grows the receptive field linearly in L, and every layer you add costs parameters and latency.
Stride and dilation both widen the receptive field without adding either. So we can see more context without a bigger model.

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
section: Depthwise convolution, and why more FLOPs does not mean faster inference
text:
Depthwise convolution, and why more FLOPs does not mean faster inference
Depthwise convolutions have more wall-clock time. The reason is arithmetic intensity: operations performed per byte moved. Each depthwise weight gets used once per spatial position and then discarded, so there is almost no reuse and the layer sits memory bound.
There is a second problem. A depthwise layer is thin in the information sense, because each output channel only ever looks at one input channel.
MobileNetV2 fixes both with the inverted bottleneck:
input (C channels)
  -> 1x1 conv        (expand to C x t channels)
  -> depthwise conv
  -> 1x1 conv        (project down to C_out)
The expansion ratio t is 6 in MobileNetV2.






Why “inverted”



A classical bottleneck squeezes and then expands. This one expands and then squeezes, which is the reverse, hence the name. The expand step has to write more data to memory and the project step has to read more, so in practice the three are fused into a single kernel.

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
Normalization and activations
Normalize to mean 0, variance 1:
\hat{x}_i = \frac{x_i - \mu_i}{\sigma_i}
Batch norm computes statistics per channel. Layer norm computes them across the channel dimension.



Activation
Definition




Sigmoid
1 / (1 + e^{-x})


ReLU
\max(0, x)


ReLU6
\min(\max(0, x), 6)


Leaky ReLU
\max(ax, x)


Swish
x / (1 + e^{-x})


Hard swish
x \cdot \text{ReLU6}(x + 3) / 6









ReLU6 and hard swish are not arbitrary



Both exist because of quantization. ReLU6 bounds the activation range, which makes the range easy to represent in fixed point. Hard swish replaces a sigmoid with clamped arithmetic, so there is no transcendental function to approximate on an integer unit.

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
What “efficient” actually means
Split the metrics into two families.
Memory related: number of parameters, model size, peak number of activations.
Computation related: MACs, FLOPs, OPs.
Then two timing notions that people confuse:- Latency is the delay for one specific task. Throughput is the rate at which data gets processed. Parallelism buys you throughput; it does not necessarily buy you latency.
A useful first-order model:
\text{Latency} \approx \max(T_{\text{computation}}, T_{\text{memory}})
where
T_{\text{computation}} = \frac{\text{number of ops}}{\text{ops per second the processor can do}}
T_{\text{memory}} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{model size}}{\text{memory bandwidth}}}_{\text{moving weights}} + \underbrace{\frac{\text{input} + \text{output activations}}{\text{memory bandwidth}}}_{\text{moving activations}}






The line most people get backwards



On IoT and microcontroller inference, the memory bottleneck is the peak activation count, not the parameter count. Early layers carry large activations because the spatial resolution is high. Later layers carry large weights because the channel count is high. If you only ever look at parameter counts, you will optimize the wrong half of the network.

title: Efficient ML, Part 1: The Primitives and the Metrics
text:
MAC arithmetic
A multiply-accumulate is a \leftarrow a \cdot b + c.

Matrix-vector product: m \cdot n MACs
General matrix-matrix product (GEMM): m \cdot n \cdot k MACs

Per layer:







Layer
MACs




Linear
C_o \cdot C_i


Conv
C_i \cdot k_h \cdot k_w \cdot h_o \cdot w_o \cdot C_o


Grouped conv
(C_i / g) \cdot k_h \cdot k_w \cdot h_o \cdot w_o \cdot C_o


Depthwise conv
k_h \cdot k_w \cdot h_o \cdot w_o \cdot C_o



One MAC is two FLOPs. And keep the two spellings straight: FLOPs is a count of operations, FLOPS is FLOPs per second.
Next post: pruning and sparsity.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
Pruning needs hardware support to pay off, distillation needs a teacher, but dropping FP32 to INT8 gives you a 4x smaller model on hardware that already exists. That’s the best part about quantization.
First the basics:

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
Number formats
Integers. Unsigned covers 0 to 2^n - 1. Signed magnitude covers -(2^{n-1} - 1) to 2^{n-1} - 1, and nobody uses it, because it burns a bit on the sign and gives you two representations of zero. Two’s complement covers -2^{n-1} to 2^{n-1} - 1 and wastes nothing.
Fixed point. A sign bit, then an integer field, then a fraction field. The binary point sits at a position you choose once and never move.
Floating point. A sign bit, an exponent field, and a fraction field:
(-1)^{\text{sign}} \times 2^{\text{exp} - 127} \times (1 + \text{fraction})
FP32 gives 1 bit of sign, 8 of exponent, 23 of fraction. The 127 is the exponent bias, present so a single unsigned 8-bit field can express both positive and negative exponents.
When the exponent field is all zeros you are in subnormal territory, and the implicit leading 1 disappears:
(-1)^{\text{sign}} \times \text{fraction} \times 2^{1 - 127}






Exponent buys range, fraction buys precision



This one sentence explains the entire FP16 versus BF16 argument.



Format
Sign
Exponent
Fraction




FP32
1
8
23


FP16
1
5
10


BF16
1
8
7



BF16 keeps FP32’s exponent width and throws away fraction bits. It trades FP16’s extra precision for a wider dynamic range. That is exactly the trade you want in training, where gradients underflow FP16’s narrow range but nobody needs 23 bits of mantissa.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
K-means quantization
Cluster the weights, store the centroids in a codebook, and replace each weight with its cluster index. A codebook of length n means n clusters. The weights become integers; the codebook stays floating point; the activations stay floating point.
Do the arithmetic. With M parameters and N-bit indices, where M \gg 2^N:

FP32 storage: 32M bits
K-means storage: NM bits, plus 32 \cdot 2^N bits of codebook, which is negligible

So you shrink by 32/N.
Fine-tuning the centroids is neat. Compute the gradients as usual, group them by cluster, average within each group, and subtract that average from the corresponding centroid. This prevents from training millions of weights.
How many bits do you need? The empirical answer from Deep Compression: 4 bits for convolutional weights, 2 bits for fully connected layers. FC layers are more redundant.
You can squeeze further with Huffman coding: fewer bits for weights that occur often, more for the rare ones.






What K-means quantization does not give you



It saves only storage not compute. At inference you decompress the weights through a lookup table, filling in the centroid for each cluster index, and then you do exactly the same floating point computation as before. It is used when weights are the bottleneck and compute is not, which describes a lot of LLM serving. Ex: Llama 7B

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
Linear quantization
This is the one that changes the arithmetic. Weights become integers and so do activations, which means the multiply-accumulate itself runs on integer hardware.
The affine mapping between a real value r and its quantized integer q:
r = S(q - Z)
S = \frac{r_{\max} - r_{\min}}{q_{\max} - q_{\min}}, \qquad Z = \text{round}\left(q_{\min} - \frac{r_{\min}}{S}\right)
S is the scale and Z is the zero point.
If we write y, x and W in terms of q and Z: q_y can be computed using only linear matrix multiplication in q_x and q_W, with no floating point operations required. That gives us integer-only inference.






Two implementation details that matter



The rescaling factor that appears in the derivation is floating point, which would spoil the whole exercise. TFLite avoids it by approximating the multiplication and division as 2^{-n}, which is a bit shift.
And the accumulation is done in a 32-bit accumulator. You quantize to 8 bits, but the sum of many 8-bit products needs headroom, so the running sum lives in INT32 and gets requantized at the end.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
Granularity
The coarser your scale, the fewer scale factors to store and the worse the fit to the actual distribution. Per-tensor is cheapest, per-channel is standard, per-group is finer still.
Group quantization uses one scale per small group of elements within a channel.
Multi-level scaling is the idea unifying VSQuant and MX:
r = (q - Z) \cdot S_{l_0} \cdot S_{l_1}

S_{l_0} is fine level, covering a small group, and is cheap and low precision
S_{l_1} is coarse level, covering a large group, and is expensive and high precision

VS-Quant is the two-level version: a per-channel float scale \gamma multiplied by a per-vector integer scale.
r = \gamma \, S_q (q - Z)
Count the bits. Four-bit weights, plus a 4-bit scale shared across 16 elements, gives 4 + 4/16 = 4.25 bits per weight.
MX (shared microexponent) data types push the same idea further. MX4 is S1M2, meaning 1 sign bit and 2 mantissa bits. Then every 2 elements share one E1M0, and every 16 elements share one E8M0.
3 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{8}{16} = 4 \text{ bits per element}

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
section: Finding the clipping range for activations
text:
Finding the clipping range for activations
Weights you can inspect directly. Activations you cannot, because they depend on the input. So you have to estimate the dynamic range, and there are two moments to do it.
During training. Track an exponential moving average of the min and max, updating after each batch’s forward pass. The smoothing matters; you do not want one outlier batch setting your range forever.
After training. Run a calibration dataset through the model and take the mean of the observed min and max. Or be smarter about it.

The KL divergence method
The dilemma:

Clip too aggressively and you lose information at the tails, producing large quantization errors on outliers.
Clip too loosely and you waste your quantization steps on a range that is mostly empty.

KL divergence, also called relative entropy or information divergence, measures the information lost when you approximate one distribution with another:
D_{KL}(P \| Q) = \sum_i^N P(x_i) \log \frac{P(x_i)}{Q(x_i)}
So choose the clipping threshold that minimizes the KL divergence between the original FP32 distribution and the resulting INT8 distribution. This is what TensorRT does.
An alternative is to minimize MSE directly, solving with Newton-Raphson. The OCTAV method finds these optimal scalars on the fly, which improves quantization-aware training.


Clipping inside QAT

EMA, as above: update the global min and max by exponential moving average after each batch.
PACT (learnable clipping): make the clipping threshold a parameter and let backpropagation find it.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
AdaRound
The problem with Round-to-nearest: RTN introduces error in a consistent direction. Sometimes rounding 2.6 down to 2 lets the error cancel against errors elsewhere and produces a better final output than rounding it up to 3.
So we make the rounding decision learnable:
w_q = s \cdot \left( \lfloor \tilde{w} \rfloor + V \right), \qquad V = h(v) = \text{sigmoid}(v)
V should end up at 0 or 1, but a sigmoid gives you a continuous value in between, which is what makes it differentiable. The loss:
L = \arg\min \|Wx - W_q(v)x\|_F^2 + \lambda f_{\text{reg}}(v)
The first term compares the FP32 layer output against the output using quantized weights. The regularization term pushes the sigmoid towards a hard 0 or 1 so you end up with an actual rounding decision.






Scope of AdaRound



It applies to weights only, and it is a post-training quantization technique. Note that calibration data is now doing double duty: AdaRound uses it for the weights, and range estimation uses it for the activations.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
Quantization-aware training
PTQ eventually runs out of room, usually below 8 bits. Then you train with quantization in the loop.
Forward pass through layer N:
W -> Q(W) ---|
             v
Q(X) ---> [ Layer N ] ---> y ---> Q(y) ---> to layer N+1
The awkward part is the backward pass, because Q(\cdot) has zero gradient almost everywhere and is undefined at the step edges. The straight-through estimator simply pretends the quantizer is the identity function:
g_y = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Q(y)} \approx \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}
and likewise through Q(W):
g_W = g_y \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial Q(W)}
The update is applied to the full precision weights, not the quantized ones:
\hat{W} = W - \gamma \, g_W






Why keep full precision weights around during QAT?





Because the quantized weights sit on a coarse grid. A gradient step small enough to be useful would round straight back to the same grid point and nothing would ever change. Keeping a shadow copy in FP32 lets many small updates accumulate until the weight genuinely crosses to the next quantization level.

title: Efficient ML, Part 3: Quantization
text:
The extreme end
Binarization maps weights to \{-1, +1\}. Ternarization adds zero, giving \{-1, 0, +1\}. Either way, multiply the whole matrix by a single scale to reduce the error, and the standard choice of scale is the mean absolute value of the original weights.
Binarization comes in two flavours: deterministic, where the sign decides, and stochastic, where the value determines a probability of mapping to +1.
Mixed precision quantization takes the sane middle road: use different bit widths for different layers, roughly 1 to 8 bits, and search the assignment with reinforcement learning. Not every layer is equally sensitive, and treating them uniformly leaves accuracy on the table.
Next in this series: what all this looks like on a microcontroller.

text: I still have so much to share. So here we go…..

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
section: 6. Residual Connections: The Real Story is in the Backward Pass
text:
6. Residual Connections: The Real Story is in the Backward Pass
class ResidualConnection(nn.Module):
    '''Solves the vanishing gradient problem'''
    def __init__(self, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout=nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.norm=LayerNormalisation()
    
    def forward(self, x, sublayer):
        return x+self.dropout(sublayer(self.norm(x)))

A Major change in modern approach from the 2017 paper:






Pre-LN vs Post-LN



self.norm(x) happens before sublayer(...), and the result is added to the untouched x. That’s:
\[x_{l+1} = x_l + \text{Dropout}(\text{Sub}(\text{LN}(x_l)))\]
This is Pre-LN, not the Post-LN of the original 2017 paper (LN(x + Sub(x))). Why did we do this? What is warm-up? How does it helps? Mathematical explanation and my experiment to prove it in the linked blog: [link].

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
section: 7. Assembling the Blocks: Why Dependency Injection?
text:
7. Assembling the Blocks: Why Dependency Injection?
class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, self_attention_block: MultiHeadAttention, ff_block: FeedForwardBlock, dropout: float):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attention_block = self_attention_block
        self.ff_block = ff_block
        self.residual_connections = nn.ModuleList([ResidualConnection(dropout) for _ in range(2)])

    def forward(self, x: Tensor, src_mask: Tensor = None):
        x = self.residual_connections[0](x, lambda x: self.self_attention_block(x, x, x, src_mask))
        x = self.residual_connections[1](x, self.ff_block)
        return x
Here we make the design choice of constructor injection for Flexibility (a custom attention variant can be swapped in) instead of the internal-init alternative which leads to tight coupling.






Knowledge point :- choosing batch size



Increasing batch_size -> the model updates after seeing more data per step -> less noisy gradient estimates but more compute and memory per step (with diminishing returns past a point).
Smaller batch_size -> more noise to the gradient -> makes training less stable.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
text:
8. Two Kinds of Masks
Inside the encoder and decoder layer, we use masking to compute attention of only the tokens that is needed
The encoder uses a padding mask, the decoder block uses two structurally different masks:









Causal / look-ahead mask
Padding mask




Applied in
Self-attention (Q=K=V=x)
Cross-attention (Q=decoder, K=V=enc_out)


Masks
Future target tokens
Padding tokens in the source


Shape
Triangular, (seq_len, seq_len)
Flat, (1, src_len)


Purpose
Force autoregressive behavior -> no cheating by looking ahead
Ignore meaningless padding positions


Changes per batch?
No -> same triangle every time
Yes -> depends on each sentence’s real length

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
text:
9. Wiring It All Together
def build_transformer(src_vocab_size, tgt_vocab_size, src_seq_len, tgt_seq_len,
                       d_model=512, N=6, h=8, d_ff=2048, dropout=0.1):
    ...
    for w in transformer.parameters():
        if w.dim() > 1:
            nn.init.xavier_uniform_(w)
    return transformer
Every multi-dimensional parameter (weight matrices, not biases :- w.dim() > 1 filters those out) gets Xavier-uniform init, which scales initial weights based on fan-in/fan-out to keep activation variance roughly stable across layers at the start of training.






Knowledge point :- Xavier initialization



To calculate the ideal starting weights, Xavier initialization relies on two structural properties of the layer:

fan_in: The number of input connections (neurons) entering the layer.
fan_out: The number of output connections leaving the layer.

Depending on the distribution you choose, the weights are drawn as follows:
1. Xavier Normal Initialization Weights are drawn from a Normal (Gaussian) distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) of:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\text{fan\_in} + \text{fan\_out}}}\]
2. Xavier Uniform Initialization Weights are drawn from a Uniform distribution bounded between \([-x, x]\), where \(x\) is:
\[x = \sqrt{\frac{6}{\text{fan\_in} + \text{fan\_out}}}\]
(Note: This is commonly applied exclusively to multi-dimensional weight matrices; 1-dimensional biases are typically initialized to zero).
The Exception: It does not work well with ReLU or its variants (Leaky ReLU, GELU), because ReLU zeros out half of the distribution, cutting the variance in half. He Initialization (Kaiming initialization) works with ReLU-based networks as it adjusts the numerator to account for the dead neurons.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
section: 10. Training Loop: Loss function, Label Smoothing, and Checkpointing
text:
10. Training Loop: Loss function, Label Smoothing, and Checkpointing
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=tokenizer_src.token_to_id('[pad]'), label_smoothing=0.1).to(device)
label_smoothing=0.1 takes some probability mass away from the “correct” token and spreads it across the rest of the vocabulary, so the model prevented from being over-confident.
ignore_index on the pad token keeps padding positions out of the loss entirely, since they carry no real supervision signal.






Knowledge point :- Warmup and Noam schedule



The paper’s Noam schedule is:
\[\text{lr} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(\text{step}^{-0.5},\ \text{step} \cdot \text{warmup}^{-1.5})\]
linear ramp-up for the first warmup_steps, then inverse-square-root decay. This is done because it’s the direct fix for the Post-LN problem from §6. More on warmup in [Link]


train.py was also equipped to handle crash recovery from last checkpoint.
I used greedy decoding for inference, but beam search is a common alternative. More on that in later blogs.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
section: ⭐ Honourable mentions: Dropout layers (They are everywhere !!!)
text:
⭐ Honourable mentions: Dropout layers (They are everywhere !!!)
While writting the code, I found we were using dropout in every next layer. So I set out to understand it’s implementation and use of every single dropout.

1. After Positional Encoding
Applied on the sum of token embeddings + positional encodings.
Forces the model not to over-rely on any specific position or embedding dimension right from the start - regularizes the input before it enters the encoder/decoder stack.

Paper (Section 5.4): “we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings.”




2. On Attention Weights (inside Attention block)
Applied after softmax, before multiplying by V.
After softmax, each row is a probability distribution over all tokens. Without dropout, the model can memorize which tokens to always attend to (attention collapse). Dropout randomly zeroes out weights, forcing the model to spread attention and learn more robust, distributed patterns.



3. In Residual Connection block (On Sublayer Output)
def forward(self, x, sublayer):
    return x + self.dropout(sublayer(self.norm(x)))
Applied on the output of each sublayer (Attention or FeedForward), before adding back to the residual stream.
The sublayer output is the new information being added to the residual stream
Dropping parts of it forces the model not to rely too heavily on any single transformation

Paper: “We apply dropout to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input.”




4. Inside FeedForward - Between the Two Linear Layers (Modern Addition)
def forward(self, x):
    x = F.relu(self.linear1(x))   # d_model → d_ff
    x = self.dropout(x)            # NOT in original paper
    x = self.linear2(x)            # d_ff → d_model
    return x
Not in the original paper - added in modern implementations.
The FFN expands to 4× the model size internally (d_ff = 4 × d_model).
In this large intermediate space, neurons can co-adapt - always firing together to produce memorized patterns.
The Residual Connection’s dropout acts on the final compressed output and cannot prevent co-adaptation forming inside the FFN. Internal dropout breaks this by regularizing the expanded space directly.



Full Dropout Flow
Token IDs
    │
[Text Encoding]               ← no dropout
    │
    + [Positional Encoding]
    │
[Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #1: input representation
    │
┌───────── Encoder Layer ──────────┐
│                                  │
│  [LayerNorm]                     │
│      │                           │
│  [Attention]                     │
│      │                           │
│  [Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #2: attention weights (inside Attention)
│      │                           │
│  [Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #3: sublayer output (inside Residual)
│      │                           │
│   x + sublayer(x)               │
│                                  │
│  (same structure for FFN layer)  │
│                                  │
│  [Dropout] ◄─────────────────── #4: inside FFN between linears (modern only)
│                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────┘


Hyperparameter
All dropout locations share the same p value:

Base model: p = 0.1
Large model: p = 0.3

It is a single hyperparameter tuned across the entire architecture.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log [Part-2]
text:
Loose Threads
A couple of things that came up while reading through this code but don’t belong in the transformer itself - they’re the next two things on my list:






Knowledge point :- KV cache



Generating M new tokens with a prompt of length N naively costs O(M · (N+M)²). Caching the key/value states from previous steps drops the incremental per-token cost to O(1) relative to history length, since only the new token’s K/V needs computing.








Knowledge point :- attention memory and FlashAttention



Storing the full [B, H, S, S] attention score matrix for the backward pass is O(S²) memory. This is what makes long-context training memory-bound rather than compute-bound, and it’s exactly the problem FlashAttention is built to avoid by never materializing the full matrix.



Source: Github repo

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
There’s no shortage of transformer tutorials floating around. It’s the most basic deep learning architecture in NLP today, so why bother building one from scratch again?
Because it’s exactly that: the basic building block for almost every architecture running today. I spend my actual working hours around fast-conformer models and diffusion models, but actually building this basic transformer with my own hands (and several 2am debugging sessions) turned out to be very different and suprisingly very insightful. Enough that I decided I had to write a log about it.
So here’s that log. I built an encoder-decoder transformer straight from the original paper, trained it on opus_books for English to Italian translation, and kept a running list of every question that had me pausing mid-line wondering what the authors were thinking.
The source lives in four files: model.py for the architecture, dataset.py for the data pipeline, config.py for the hyperparameters, and train.py for the training loop. code link

text:
There’s no shortage of transformer tutorials floating around. It’s the most basic deep learning architecture in NLP today, so why bother building one from scratch again?
Because it’s exactly that: the basic building block for almost every architecture running today. I spend my actual working hours around fast-conformer models and diffusion models, but actually building this basic transformer with my own hands (and several 2am debugging sessions) turned out to be very different and suprisingly very insightful. Enough that I decided I had to write a log about it.
So here’s that log. I built an encoder-decoder transformer straight from the original paper, trained it on opus_books for English to Italian translation, and kept a running list of every question that had me pausing mid-line wondering what the authors were thinking.
The source lives in four files: model.py for the architecture, dataset.py for the data pipeline, config.py for the hyperparameters, and train.py for the training loop. code link

Architecture at a Glance
Six encoder blocks feed a stack of six decoder blocks through cross-attention, exactly as in the 2017 paper. d_model = 512, h = 8 heads, d_ff = 2048, max_seq_len = 350, dropout = 0.1.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 1. Text Embeddings: Turning Tokens Into Vectors
text:
1. Text Embeddings: Turning Tokens Into Vectors
Let \(W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{model}}\) be the learnable embedding weight matrix.
The text embedding formula for a given token at position \(pos\) with vocabulary index \(k\) is: \[E_{pos} = W_E[k] \cdot \sqrt{d_{model}}\]
nn.Embedding is just a lookup table: [vocab_size, d_model], initialized randomly and learned during training. During forward pass :- [batch, seq_len] -> [batch, seq_len, d_model]






Q1: Why multiply by √d_model?



The positional encodings (next section) have values bounded in [-1, 1]. Raw embeddings, especially right after Xavier init, sit at a much smaller scale.
√d_model scale-up the text embeddings that becomes comparable to the additive positional signal early in training.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
section: 2. Positional Encoding: Giving the Model a Sense of Order
text:
2. Positional Encoding: Giving the Model a Sense of Order
Formulas:-
For even dimensions (\(2i\)): \[PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_{model}}}}\right)\] For odd dimensions (\(2i + 1\)): \[PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\frac{2i}{d_{model}}}}\right)\] \(i\) is a specific feature dimension (where \(i\) goes from \(0\) to \(d_{model}/2\))






Positional Encoding: Use of sin and cos



The maths behind chosing sin and cos, it’s pros and cons and recent advancements in positional encoding is discussed in my other blog: [link: to be done]


Two implementation details:

register_buffer, not nn.Parameter: Registering in buffer allows the deterministic embeddings that never gets trained to be moved with the model across .to(device) calls and be saved/restored in state_dict().
The e^(ln(A)B) trick:  10000^(-2i/d_model) is computed as exp(-2i/d_model * ln(10000)) because torch.pow on a fractional, negative exponent across a whole tensor is less numerically stable than composing exp and log, which PyTorch has fast, stable kernels for.

\[X_{final} = \text{Dropout}\Big( E_{pos} + PE_{pos} \Big)\]






Knowledge point :- Use of dropout across the Transformer paper



The information in the original paper is a bit scattered, so here’s a summary of where dropout is applied: Link

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
3. LayerNorm From Scratch






Q2: What is the use of Normalization?



As data moves non-linear activations and weight multiplications leads to Internal Covariate Shift.

The variance of the activations grows too large -> the gradients explode
It shrinks too much -> the gradients vanish
Normalization solves this by forcing the activations back to a standard scale (typically a mean of 0 and a variance of 1) at every layer. The general mathematical formula for normalization is: \[y = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta\]









Q3: Why LayerNorm and why not BatchNorm?



BatchNorm normalizes across batch dimension and assumes batch statistics are stable and representative. Two things break that assumption here:

Variable sequence lengths + padding:  Batch statistics get polluted by padding tokens that are used to fill sequences to the same length.
Batch size of 1 at inference: BatchNorm’s statistics are undefined (or at best a single noisy sample) at batch size 1.

LayerNorm is better here because it normalizes across the feature dimension (d_model) independently per token, so it behaves identically whether the batch is 1 sentence or 64.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
4. Multi-Head Attention
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

q, k, v start as [batch, seq_len, d_model].

Then first it is converted to [batch, seq_len, h, d_k] (d_k = d_model/h)

And then transposed to[batch, h, seq_len, d_k]
WHY???? -> Allows each head to take info from all the seq tokens
After attention, .transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(...) merges the heads back. .contiguous() is required here because .transpose returns a view with non-contiguous memory, and .view() refuses to operate on that.







Q4: Why divide by √d_k? What happens if you don’t?



Assume the components of q and k are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1 (a reasonable approximation right after Xavier/careful init). The dot product q·k sums d_k such independent products, so its variance grows to Var(q·k) ≈ d_k - the standard deviation grows as √d_k.
And when passed through softmax, it is exponentiated and output collapse towards one-hot. (ex output: [0.999, 0.001, 0.000]) The gradient of softmax with respect to its logits is roughly p(1-p), which is near zero for entries pinned near 0 or 1. So your gradients completely die. Your model just sits there, learning nothing.
Dividing by √d_k renormalizes the dot product back to unit variance regardless of d_k and prevents gradient collapse.

title: Building the Transformer From Scratch: An Implementation Log
text:
5. The FeedForward Block
Two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between. (512 -> 2048 -> RELU -> 512) FFN(x) = max(0, W·x + b1)W2 + b2 This block is applied pointwise.
Each token, in isolation, does its own nonlinear processing on what it just gathered.






Q5: Why is there dropout inside the FFN in modern approaches?



The dropout inside the FFN, between linear_1 and linear_2, is a modern addition.
Why it matters: d_ff is 4× d_model. Here, neurons can co-adapt (learn to always fire together to reproduce memorized patterns). A dropout is applied in the residual connection but it only acts on the compressed final output and can’t see or break up that internal co-adaptation. Internal FFN dropout regularizes the expanded space directly.







Scenario
Internal FFN dropout needed?




Small model, small d_ff
Not much, residual dropout is enough


Large model, large d_ff
Yes, co-adaptation risk grows with size


Fine-tuning on small datasets
Yes, overfitting risk is real


Large-scale pretraining
Often removed, data volume is the regularizer

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
Three techniques dominate model compression: pruning, distillation, and quantization. This post covers the first.
The loop is simple: (one pass is never enough)

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
What pruning is, formally
\arg\min_{W_p} \; L_0(x; W_p) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|W_p\|_0 \le N
The loss L is whatever you trained with, cross-entropy or MSE. The L_0 norm counts non-zero elements in a tensor, so N is the surviving parameters.






Read more



The L_0, L_1, and L_2 norms all show up in this context: L_0 as the sparsity constraint, L_1 as the importance criterion in network slimming, L_2 as the magnitude criterion.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
section: Granularity, and the trap in it
text:
Granularity, and the trap in it
Pruning granularity runs along a spectrum, from picking off individual weights to deleting whole channels:








Granularity
What gets removed
Accelerable?




Fine-grained / unstructured
Individual weights, anywhere
Hard, the pattern is irregular


Pattern-based (N:M)
Fixed count per block, indices stored
Yes, with hardware support


Vector level
Contiguous runs within a row
Partially


Kernel level
Whole k_h \times k_w kernels
Better


Channel level
Whole input or output channels
Yes, it stays a dense tensor









Fewer parameters does not mean more speed



Unstructured pruning can throw away 90% of your weights and leave inference exactly as slow as before, because the surviving weights sit in irregular positions and your GEMM kernel cannot exploit that. Channel pruning removes less but the result is a smaller dense tensor, which every piece of hardware already knows how to multiply quickly.


N:M sparsity is the compromise. In each contiguous block of M elements, N of them are pruned. The common case is 2:4, giving 50% sparsity, which is what Nvidia’s sparse tensor cores support.
For channel pruning you can either shrink every layer uniformly or assign each layer its own sparsity ratio. The second is better. Finding those ratios is the hard part.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
Which weights to remove
Element-wise. Importance is |W|. Small weights go.
Row-wise. Importance is \sum_i |w_i| (an L_1 norm) or the row-wise L_2 norm \sqrt{\sum_i |w_i|^2}.
Scaling-factor based (network slimming). Attach a trainable scaling factor to each filter, meaning each output channel. Add an L_1 penalty on those factors during training, then prune the channels whose factor stayed small. The neat trick here is that you do not need a new parameter: reuse the scaling factor that batch norm already gives you.
Percentage of zeros (APoZ). For channels sitting behind a ReLU, measure how often the output is zero. A channel that is almost always zero is not contributing.
Regression based. Instead of measuring the error in the objective function, minimize the error in each layer’s output after pruning:
L = \arg\min \|Z - Z'\|^2
You keep a coefficient vector \beta over channels, where \beta_i = 0 means channel i is pruned. Solve it by alternating: fix W and solve for \beta, then fix \beta and solve for W to minimize reconstruction error. This layer-wise reconstruction idea is exactly what modern LLM compression methods use.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
Choosing the ratio per layer
Sensitivity analysis. Prune one layer at a time, sweep the ratio, plot accuracy against ratio. Pick a \DeltaAcc threshold and read off the ratio each layer can tolerate.






Where sensitivity analysis breaks



Each curve is measured with every other layer left intact, so interactions between layers are invisible.
Worse, the plot has no notion of layer size. A layer you can prune 80% of might hold 2% of the parameters, in which case pruning it aggressively buys you almost nothing.


Two automated alternatives:

AMC, AutoML for Model Compression, which searches the per-layer ratios with reinforcement learning.
NetAdapt, which is iterative rather than learned.

Both beat uniform pruning on the accuracy-versus-latency curve, and both are worth reading in full.






Why does channel pruning give superlinear FLOP reduction?





Because pruning a conv layer reduces both its input channels and the previous layer’s output channels. The MAC count is proportional to C_i \cdot C_o, so a reduction on both sides multiplies. Cut both by a factor r and FLOPs fall by r^2. This is why channel pruning ratios that sound modest produce speedups that sound implausible.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
Fine-tuning after pruning
Add regularization to the loss term, and drop the learning rate to a tenth or a hundredth of the original to recover the accuracy lost.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
section: Making sparsity pay off in hardware
text:
Making sparsity pay off in hardware
Software alone will not cash in unstructured sparsity. EIE, the Efficient Inference Engine, is the classic accelerator design that does, and it exploits three separate facts:








Exploit
Reasoning
Gain claimed




Sparse weights
0 \times A = 0, skip the MAC
10x less computation, 5x less memory


Sparse activations
W \times 0 = 0, skip the MAC
3x less computation


Weight sharing
Store a 4-bit index, not a 32-bit float
8x less memory



The memory saving from sparse weights is smaller than the compute saving because you now have to store indices alongside values.
Storage format. Weights go in compressed sparse column form, which is three arrays: the non-zero values, a relative index (how many zeros preceded each value in its column), and a column pointer marking where each column’s run begins. The pointer array is built by running addition: each entry is the previous pointer plus the count of non-zeros in that column.
Worked on the matrix from the lecture, taking the two rows assigned to PE0:
\text{row}_0 = [2, -1, 0, 0], \qquad \text{row}_4 = [0, 3, -2, 0]




col 0
col 1
col 2
col 3




Values
2
−1, 3
−2
(none)


Relative index
0
0, 0
1



Column pointer
0
1
3
4, then 4



Parallelization. Rows of W are dealt out to processing elements round-robin, so PE0 gets rows 0 and 4, PE1 gets rows 1 and 5, and so on. Everything lives in SRAM; EIE never goes to DRAM.
The pipeline inside a PE:
Leading Non-Zero Detection (LNZD)
  -> broadcast to the activation queue of each PE, via the Central Control Unit
  -> Pointer Read Unit
  -> Sparse Matrix Read Unit
  -> Weight Decode
  -> Arithmetic Unit (performs the MAC)
  -> Activation Read/Write Unit
  -> ReLU, then LNZD again for the next layer
The activation queue is doing real work here: it smooths load imbalance between processing elements, since different rows have different numbers of non-zeros.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
text:
Sparsity in modern workloads
Sparsity is not only a weight phenomenon. Different domains hand you different kinds for free:

Transformers: token sparsity
Video: temporal sparsity, because most objects did not move between frames
Point clouds: spatial sparsity, most of the volume is empty
Generative vision models: spatial sparsity

Nvidia’s hardware path for M:N sparsity converts the pruned weight matrix into a non-zero value matrix plus an index matrix. At runtime a multiplexer uses those indices to select the matching activations, and the dense non-zero matrix is multiplied against them.

title: Efficient ML, Part 2: Pruning and Sparsity
section: A closing warning about sparse convolution
text:
A closing warning about sparse convolution
The naive approach on point clouds is to compute the convolution at position (i, j) only when input[i][j] is non-zero. That works, but it destroys regularity: different weights end up interacting with different input patterns, and memory access becomes unpredictable.
TorchSparse takes the opposite tack. It adds padding back into the features so the computation regains a regular shape, accepting some wasted work in exchange for access patterns the hardware can actually stream. That trade, a little redundant computation for a lot of regularity, shows up over and over once you start looking for it.
Next in this series: quantization.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text: Everything in the previous three posts was general. This one is about the actually deploying the model on the hardest deployment target: a microcontroller.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
The budget



Resource
Where it lives
How much




Weights
Flash / DRAM
under 1 MB


Activations
SRAM
around 360 KB



Compared against an H100 at roughly 1,979 TOPS, or a flagship phone at roughly 36 TOPS. A TinyML engine works with a few hundred kilobytes of memory and a compute budget in the hundreds of millions of operations per second.






Compute is cheap, memory is expensive



On a microcontroller the binding constraint is memory, not arithmetic. Which flips the usual optimization target: instead of minimizing FLOPs, you maximize FLOPs subject to a memory constraint, because more computation within the same memory footprint means larger model capacity, which usually means better accuracy.
This is also why MobileNetV2’s inverted bottleneck, which was a win on phones, becomes a liability here. Expanding the channel count before the depthwise convolution raises the peak activation size, and peak activation size is exactly what SRAM caps.



How the two memories trade against each other
The activation tensor occupies roughly \text{Res} \times \text{Res} \times \text{Ch} in SRAM, while the weights occupy flash. So:
Flash fixed, SRAM increased. Channel count stays put, resolution goes up. You can afford to hold larger activations.
Flash increased, SRAM fixed. Channel count and width multiplier go up, and resolution has to come down to compensate, because the SRAM product must stay constant.
Buying more storage for weights does not let you process bigger images. It lets you process smaller images with a wider network.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
Patch-based inference
The peak activation problem usually lives in the first few layers, where resolution is highest. Patch-based inference compute the network patch by patch rather than layer by layer, so only one patch’s activations need to be resident.
The cost is repeated computation, because neighbouring patches have overlapping receptive fields and the overlap gets computed twice. Roughly 10% overhead.
The fix is network redistribution: reduce the receptive field in the starting layers, where patches overlap, and increase it in the ending layers to compensate. You are moving the receptive field to where it does not cost you.
Push that further and you get MCUNetV2, which searches the neural architecture and the inference schedule jointly rather than fixing one and optimizing the other.
What actually runs on these devices:



Task
Approach




Face detection and small vision tasks
MCUNet


Small keyword detection in speech
CNN based, MCUNet


Anomaly detection
Autoencoders

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
Instruction-level parallelism
An ISA (instruction set architecture) is the vocabulary the processor understands: ADD, COMPARE, JUMP, JUMP IF, and so on. Two philosophies:
CISC, as in Intel, where one instruction does a lot:
add a, b, c
RISC, as in Arm, where each instruction does one thing:
load  a, reg1
load  b, reg2
add   reg1, reg2 -> reg3
store reg3, c
SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) applies one instruction to several data elements at once. A single add can operate on four 32-bit blocks simultaneously. It needs vector registers and vector operations in the ISA, and it buys throughput, speed, and energy efficiency at once, since you amortize one instruction fetch and decode over many operands.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
Thread-level parallelism
Threads share code, data, and files, but each gets its own registers and stack. For a matrix multiply the natural split is by rows: give each thread a slice. Use pthreads or OpenMP.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
Inference optimizations

1. Image to column (im2col)
Rearrange the input patches into columns so the convolution becomes a single matrix multiplication:
\underbrace{[HW \times K^2C]}_{\text{rearranged input}} \times \underbrace{[K^2C \times N]}_{\text{kernels}} = \underbrace{[HW \times N]}_{\text{output}}
where N is the number of kernels.
The advantage is that you get to use a GEMM routine, and GEMM is the most heavily optimized function in computing. The disadvantage is extra memory, since every input element gets replicated into multiple columns. On a microcontroller that memory does not exist, so the fix is to build the columns on the fly and multiply as you go instead of materializing the whole matrix.


2. In-place depthwise convolution
Depthwise convolution touches one channel at a time, so with channel-wise computation you can write the output back over the input and avoid holding both. Use NCHW layout for this, since it keeps each channel contiguous.


3. Layout per operation
NHWC for pointwise convolution, NCHW for depthwise convolution. Pointwise convolution walks across channels at a fixed spatial location, so NHWC makes that access sequential.






Why does layout choice matter so much here?





There is no large cache to rescue a bad access pattern. An L1 cache on these devices is on the order of 8 KB. On a server you can write cache-hostile code and lose maybe 2x. Here the memory system is the entire performance story, so matching the layout to the loop order is not a micro-optimization, it is the optimization.





4. Winograd convolution
A fast convolution algorithm that trades multiplications for additions. Worth reading separately.

title: Efficient ML, Part 4: TinyML on Microcontrollers
text:
Where this post ends up
As I went through this series of lectures I learned about handling constraints, realized that bigger models may not be the future in applications and there might not exist a perfect solution. Almost every technique I learned is a trade between how much you compute and how predictably you can move data.
Depthwise convolution wins on FLOPs and loses on arithmetic intensity. Unstructured pruning wins on parameter count and loses on regularity. Patch-based inference accepts 10% redundant computation to fit in SRAM. TorchSparse pads a sparse tensor back towards density for the same reason.
Counting operations and metrices is the easy part. Knowing when the count is lying and how they relate is the job.
